query: What is the definition of murder under BNS?
reference_answer: Under BNS Section 101, murder is defined as culpable homicide that is committed with the intention of causing death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as the offender knows to be likely to cause the death of the person to whom the harm is caused, or with the intention of causing bodily injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, or when the person committing the act knows that it is so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death.

query: What is the punishment for murder under BNS?
reference_answer: Under BNS Section 103, whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine. In cases where the murder is committed by a group of five or more persons on specified grounds, each member of that group shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life or imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

query: What replaced Section 302 IPC?
reference_answer: Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, which dealt with punishment for murder, has been replaced by Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). BNS Section 103 similarly prescribes death or imprisonment for life, along with fine, for the offence of murder. The BNS also introduces an additional provision for group lynching scenarios not explicitly present in IPC 302.

query: What replaced Section 300 IPC?
reference_answer: Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code, which defined the offence of murder and its exceptions, has been replaced by Section 101 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). BNS Section 101 retains the essential elements of the definition of murder from IPC 300, including the four clauses relating to intention and knowledge, as well as the exceptions for grave and sudden provocation, private defence, public servant acting in good faith, and sudden fight.

query: What is the definition of rape under BNS?
reference_answer: Under BNS, rape refers to sexual intercourse with a woman under specified circumstances including against her will, without her consent, with consent obtained by threat or fear, with consent obtained by fraud or impersonation, when she is unable to understand the nature of the act, or when she is under 18 years of age. The definition emphasises the absence of free and voluntary consent as the core element of the offence.

query: What is the punishment for rape under BNS?
reference_answer: Under BNS Section 64, punishment for rape is rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than ten years, which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine. In cases of aggravated rape such as rape by a public servant, police officer, or repeat offenders, the punishment is enhanced to imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment of not less than twenty years.

query: What replaced Section 376 IPC?
reference_answer: Section 376 of the Indian Penal Code, which provided punishment for rape, has been replaced by Section 64 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). BNS Section 64 retains the minimum ten-year rigorous imprisonment for rape and life imprisonment for aggravated forms. The BNS also restructures the rape provisions with broader definitions of consent and more comprehensive aggravating circumstances.

query: What constitutes assault or criminal force on a woman under BNS?
reference_answer: BNS Section 74 deals with assault or use of criminal force to a woman with intent to outrage her modesty. It prescribes imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or fine, or both. The section covers any act of physical force or threatening gesture directed at a woman with the intention of outraging her modesty.

query: What replaced Section 354 IPC?
reference_answer: Section 354 of the Indian Penal Code, which dealt with assault or criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty, has been replaced by Section 74 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). The BNS provision similarly penalises assault or criminal force directed at a woman with intent to outrage her modesty, with imprisonment and fine as punishment.

query: How is extortion defined under BNS?
reference_answer: Under BNS Section 308, extortion is defined as intentionally putting a person in fear of injury to that person or any other, and thereby dishonestly inducing the person so put in fear to deliver to any person any property, valuable security, or anything signed or sealed which may be converted into a valuable security. The essential elements are the inducement of fear and the dishonest obtaining of property or value.

query: What is the punishment for extortion under BNS?
reference_answer: Under BNS Section 308, extortion is punishable with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. In aggravated circumstances, such as when extortion is committed by threat of grievous hurt or death, the punishment is enhanced with longer imprisonment terms.

query: What replaced Section 384 IPC?
reference_answer: Section 384 of the Indian Penal Code, which prescribed punishment for extortion, has been replaced by Section 308 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). BNS Section 308 retains the essential definition and punishment structure for extortion, including the graduated punishment provisions for aggravated forms of the offence.

query: How is theft defined under BNS?
reference_answer: Under BNS Section 303, theft is defined as dishonestly taking any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent. The act of moving such property to accomplish the taking is itself called theft. The essential elements are dishonest intention, movable property, absence of consent, and the act of moving the property.

query: What replaced Section 378 and 379 IPC?
reference_answer: Sections 378 and 379 of the Indian Penal Code, which respectively defined theft and prescribed its punishment, have been consolidated and replaced by Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). BNS Section 303 retains the definition of theft and prescribes imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or fine, or both.

query: What is culpable homicide under BNS?
reference_answer: Under BNS, culpable homicide is the act of causing death with the intention of causing death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or with the knowledge that the act is likely to cause death. Culpable homicide that amounts to murder is defined in BNS Section 101, while culpable homicide not amounting to murder attracts lesser punishment.

query: How does BNSS define a First Information Report?
reference_answer: Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), a First Information Report (FIR) is the written document prepared by the police when they receive information about the commission of a cognizable offence. The BNSS provides that such information may be given orally or in writing to an officer in charge of a police station, and if given orally it shall be reduced to writing and read over to the informant who shall sign it.

query: What are the bail provisions under BNSS for bailable offences?
reference_answer: Under BNSS, a person accused of a bailable offence has a right to be released on bail. When a person accused of or suspected of committing a bailable offence is arrested without a warrant, such a person is entitled to be released on bail. The court has discretion in fixing the amount of bail bond and may impose conditions such as surrendering passport or appearing before a police officer.

query: What is the procedure for filing a charge sheet under BNSS?
reference_answer: Under BNSS, upon completion of investigation, the police officer shall forward a report to the Magistrate empowered to take cognizance. This report, commonly called a charge sheet or police report, must include the names of the parties, the nature of the information, the names of persons appearing to be acquainted with the circumstances of the case, whether any offence appears to have been committed, and if so, by whom.

query: How does BNSS handle remand of an accused?
reference_answer: Under BNSS, a Magistrate may authorise the detention of an accused in police custody for a period not exceeding fifteen days on a request by a police officer. After the initial period of detention, the Magistrate may extend the detention in judicial custody. The total period of detention prior to filing of charge sheet cannot exceed sixty or ninety days depending on the gravity of the offence.

query: What is the procedure for taking cognizance of an offence under BNSS?
reference_answer: Under BNSS, a Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence upon receiving a police report, upon receiving a complaint of facts constituting an offence, or upon information received from any person other than a police officer. Once cognizance is taken, the Magistrate may examine the complainant and witnesses, and may issue process against the accused if there is sufficient ground to proceed.

query: What are the rights of an arrested person under BNSS?
reference_answer: Under BNSS, an arrested person has the right to be informed of the grounds of arrest, the right to be produced before a Magistrate within twenty-four hours of arrest excluding travel time, the right to have a lawyer of their choice present during interrogation, and the right to inform a nominated person of their arrest. BNSS also provides for medical examination of the arrested person.

query: What is the default bail provision under BNSS if charge sheet is not filed in time?
reference_answer: Under BNSS, if a police officer fails to file the charge sheet within the prescribed period (sixty days for offences punishable with imprisonment up to ten years, and ninety days for more serious offences), the accused becomes entitled to bail as a matter of right. This is called default bail or compulsive bail, and the Magistrate is bound to release the accused on bail if the accused furnishes the required bail bond.

query: How is electronic evidence treated under BSA?
reference_answer: Under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), electronic records are admissible as documentary evidence. The BSA provides for the admissibility of electronic records, including data stored in electronic form, emails, messages, and digital documents. A certificate from a responsible official certifying that the electronic record was produced by a computer in the ordinary course of activities is required for the record to be admitted in certain circumstances.

query: What is the burden of proof under BSA?
reference_answer: Under BSA, the burden of proof in a suit or proceeding lies on the person who would fail if no evidence at all were given on either side. In criminal proceedings, the prosecution bears the burden of proving the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt. The accused may be required to prove certain matters such as exceptions or special defences on the balance of probabilities.

query: What are the rules regarding admissibility of confessions under BSA?
reference_answer: Under BSA, a confession made by an accused is relevant and may be proved against the maker. However, a confession made to a police officer is not provable against the accused. A confession made while in police custody is also inadmissible unless made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate. A co-accused's confession is admissible only as corroborative evidence and cannot be the sole basis for conviction.

query: What is the relevance of expert opinion under BSA?
reference_answer: Under BSA, when the Court has to form an opinion upon a point of foreign law, science, art, or identification of handwriting or finger impressions, opinions of persons specially skilled in such matters are relevant. Such persons are called experts. The opinion of an expert is relevant but not conclusive. The Court may accept or reject expert opinion after considering all the circumstances.

query: How does BSA define documentary evidence?
reference_answer: Under BSA, documents produced for the inspection of the Court are called documentary evidence. The BSA distinguishes between primary evidence and secondary evidence. Primary evidence means the document itself produced for the inspection of the Court. Secondary evidence includes certified copies, copies made from the original, and copies compared with the original, used when the original is unavailable.

query: What are the rules about dying declarations under BSA?
reference_answer: Under BSA, a statement made by a person as to the cause of his death, or as to any of the circumstances of the transaction which resulted in his death, made in cases in which the cause of that person's death comes into question, is a relevant fact. Such statements are called dying declarations. They are admissible regardless of whether the declarant had expectation of death at the time of making the statement.

query: What are the privileges against self-incrimination under BSA?
reference_answer: Under BSA, a witness is not excused from answering any question as to any matter relevant to the matter in issue in any suit or proceeding, except in limited circumstances. However, no such answer shall subject the witness to any arrest or prosecution, except in cases of perjury. The BSA provides certain protections to witnesses including spousal privilege and attorney-client privilege.

query: What does Article 21 of the Indian Constitution protect?
reference_answer: Article 21 of the Indian Constitution guarantees that no person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. Through judicial interpretation, the Supreme Court has expanded Article 21 to include numerous rights such as the right to live with human dignity, the right to livelihood, the right to health, the right to education, the right to privacy, and the right to a speedy trial.

query: What are the protections against arbitrary arrest under Article 22 of the Constitution?
reference_answer: Article 22 of the Indian Constitution provides protection against arbitrary arrest and detention. It guarantees the right to be informed of the grounds of arrest, the right to consult and be defended by a lawyer of choice, the right to be produced before the nearest Magistrate within twenty-four hours of arrest, and the right not to be detained beyond twenty-four hours without the authority of a Magistrate. These protections do not apply to enemy aliens or persons detained under preventive detention laws.

query: What does Article 14 of the Constitution guarantee?
reference_answer: Article 14 of the Indian Constitution guarantees equality before law and equal protection of laws within the territory of India. It prohibits the State from denying to any person equality before the law or equal protection of the laws. The Supreme Court has interpreted Article 14 to include the principle of non-arbitrariness and has struck down laws and executive actions that are arbitrary or unreasonable.

query: What is the scope of Article 19 regarding freedom of speech?
reference_answer: Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution guarantees to all citizens the right to freedom of speech and expression. This right includes the freedom to express one's views, opinions, beliefs, and convictions through any medium. However, Article 19(2) permits the State to impose reasonable restrictions on this right in the interests of sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, or in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence.

query: What is the difference between Article 32 and Article 226 writ jurisdiction?
reference_answer: Article 32 of the Constitution confers the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights and empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs including habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, and certiorari. Article 226 confers similar writ jurisdiction on High Courts but with a wider scope — High Courts can issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights as well as for any other purpose. Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right while Article 226 is a constitutional right.

query: How do Articles 15 and 16 protect against discrimination in employment?
reference_answer: Article 15 prohibits the State from discriminating against citizens on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in matters of public employment and prohibits discrimination on the same grounds in employment under the State. Article 16 also permits the State to make provisions for reservation of appointments for socially and educationally backward classes or Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

query: What is the difference between murder and culpable homicide under BNS?
reference_answer: Under BNS, culpable homicide is the genus and murder is the species. All murders are culpable homicide but not all culpable homicide amounts to murder. The distinction lies in the degree of intention and knowledge. Murder under BNS Section 101 requires a higher degree of intention or knowledge than culpable homicide not amounting to murder. Exceptions such as grave and sudden provocation, private defence, and sudden fight can reduce murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

query: How does BNS treat organised crime?
reference_answer: BNS introduces dedicated provisions dealing with organised crime syndicates, which were not comprehensively addressed in the IPC. Under BNS, organised crime includes any continuing unlawful activity carried on by an individual, singly or jointly, as a member of an organised crime syndicate. The punishment for organised crime includes death or imprisonment for life where the crime causes death, and rigorous imprisonment of not less than five years in other cases.

query: What is sedition under BNS and how has it changed from IPC?
reference_answer: The BNS does not contain the offence of sedition as it existed under Section 124A of the IPC. Instead, BNS introduces Section 152 which deals with acts endangering sovereignty, unity, and integrity of India. This section criminalises exciting or attempting to excite secession, armed rebellion, or subversive activities, as well as encouraging feelings of separatist activities. The new provision is considered broader and more specific than the colonial-era sedition provision.

query: What is the procedure for bail in non-bailable offences under BNSS?
reference_answer: Under BNSS, bail in non-bailable offences is at the discretion of the Court. The Court may grant bail to a person accused of a non-bailable offence if there are no reasonable grounds for believing the accused is guilty of such offence, or if the accused is a woman, a child, sick, or infirm. The Court must consider factors such as nature and gravity of accusation, antecedents of the accused, possibility of fleeing, and safety of the community.

query: How does BNSS provide for trial in absentia?
reference_answer: BNSS introduces provisions for trials to proceed in the absence of an accused who has absconded or evades attendance. If the Court is satisfied that an accused has absconded and there is no immediate prospect of arresting them, the Court may proceed to try such an accused person in their absence after following prescribed procedures including publication of notice and attempts to serve the accused.

query: What is the relevance of res gestae under BSA?
reference_answer: Under BSA, facts which are so connected with a fact in issue as to form part of the same transaction are relevant. This principle is known as res gestae. It includes facts forming part of the same transaction whether they occurred at the same time and place or at different times and places. This allows admission of statements and acts that are so closely connected to the transaction in question that they form part of it.

query: What digital evidence provisions does BSA introduce compared to the old Indian Evidence Act?
reference_answer: BSA significantly modernises digital evidence provisions compared to the old Indian Evidence Act. BSA provides comprehensive rules for admissibility of electronic records, including messages, emails, and computer-generated documents. It introduces the concept of electronic or digital records as primary evidence in certain circumstances, relaxes the certificate requirement in some cases, and addresses issues like hash values and metadata. The old Evidence Act had limited provisions that were later amended through the IT Act.

query: What is the significance of Article 21 in the context of undertrial prisoners?
reference_answer: The Supreme Court of India has held that Article 21's right to life and personal liberty extends to undertrial prisoners. Courts have interpreted Article 21 to include the right to speedy trial, such that prolonged pre-trial detention without trial can be a violation of Article 21. In such circumstances, undertrials may be entitled to bail. The Court has also held that the right to legal aid for undertrials is part of the Article 21 guarantee.

query: What is the doctrine of double jeopardy under the Indian Constitution?
reference_answer: Article 20(2) of the Indian Constitution provides that no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once. This is the constitutional protection against double jeopardy. For the doctrine to apply, there must have been a prior prosecution, conviction, and punishment for the same offence. The BNSS and BSA further elaborate on the procedural aspects of this protection in the context of criminal trials.

query: What is the punishment for dacoity under BNS?
reference_answer: Under BNS, dacoity is defined as robbery committed by five or more persons conjointly. The punishment for dacoity is rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, along with fine. Aggravated forms of dacoity, such as dacoity with murder, are punishable with death or imprisonment for life.

query: How does BNS define cheating?
reference_answer: Under BNS, cheating is defined as dishonestly or fraudulently deceiving any person, thereby inducing that person to deliver any property, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, or to do or omit doing something which the deceived person would not otherwise do or omit. The essential elements are the fraudulent or dishonest inducement and the delivery of property or doing of an act by the deceived person.

query: What are the provisions for anticipatory bail under BNSS?
reference_answer: Under BNSS, anticipatory bail or bail in anticipation of arrest is available under a provision similar to the former Section 438 CrPC. A person who has reason to believe they may be arrested for a non-bailable offence may apply to the Sessions Court or the High Court for a direction to be released on bail in the event of arrest. The Court considers factors such as the nature of the accusation, the applicant's antecedents, and whether the accusation is made with a view to humiliate or injure the applicant.

query: Is copyright law covered under BNS or BSA?
reference_answer: Copyright law in India is governed by the Copyright Act, 1957, which is a standalone legislation and is not covered under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) or the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA). BNS deals with general criminal offences, while BSA deals with evidence rules. Intellectual property matters including copyright are governed by their respective special statutes.
